meta.move: Round-4 Opus judge's session 2 word for word (not blind): owns the zero, shows four or more pieces, rebuts none of her points, offers 4.4
meta.expect: No deal while none of her points has been answered

turns.text: Hello, thanks for coming in. I'm Owen's English teacher.
Why am I here, Hale? Owen got a zero and nobody called me first.
Thanks for coming in. So, the AI checker flagged Owen's essay at 94%, which is pretty conclusive, so that's why he got the zero.
A machine's guess. The company that sells it says not to use it alone, so what else do you have?

Let me back up, because I started in the wrong place. I entered the zero on November 3 before calling you. Your printed procedure, 4.2, says I should have called first. That was wrong, and Owen should not have found out on his phone in class.
Okay. Now show me what you actually have, something I can check.

I'll set the checker aside; it's my weakest piece. I've turned my screen to you: this is the version history of Owen's essay. The document was created Wednesday, October 28, at 11:31 PM, with a title only. At 11:52 PM, 612 words appear in one edit. At 11:58 PM, another 794 words in one edit. Then 23 minutes of small edits to font, name and spacing. No earlier drafts.
I'm writing those times down. Owen told me he wrote it over the weekend, so he could have drafted elsewhere and pasted it in.

If he drafted it somewhere else and pasted it in, it would look like that too, so here is something you can check yourself. The essay quotes Act 3, Scene 2: "The mind that doubts is a kingdom in exile." That line is not in Hamlet. Here's the play open to 3.2. Look for it.
Give me a minute with the page. Students misquote plays every day, Hale.
And here is his outline from October 15, which he handed in himself. It argues Hamlet delays out of cowardice. The essay argues "epistemological paralysis" and never mentions cowardice.
Did anyone put these things to Owen before the zero went in? Whatever you think this is, it stays off his record.

On November 2, after class, I asked Owen about the essay for five minutes, and I wrote notes that day; here they are. Asked what "epistemological paralysis" means, he said "like, being stuck." He couldn't say which scene his second paragraph was about. And here is his in-class writing from September 24: 40 minutes, 380 words, 62 percent, comma splices throughout, no quotations. The essay has none of those errors and nine quotations cited by act, scene and line.
Five minutes after class isn't a hearing, and a seventeen-year-old lost for words isn't proof of anything. What is on his record right now?

I'm not asking you to say Owen cheated. Here's what I'm offering under procedure 4.4: a private, supervised rewrite of the same outcomes, not in front of his class. Its mark replaces the zero, and nothing goes on his record. I'll put that in writing tonight.

Fine. A private rewrite, its mark replaces the zero, nothing on his record, and it's in my inbox tonight. I'm agreeing to put this behind him, not because he did anything, and the rest goes in my email.
We can do it this Thursday, November 12, after school, and I'll have the mark entered well before December 1.
Thursday after school, then. Put that date in the email, and a date for the mark, not "well before."
Do we have an agreement?
We do: a private rewrite Thursday, its mark replaces the zero, nothing on his record, all of it in writing tonight.
END MEETING

FOLLOW-UP EMAIL
Hale,

You agreed to a private, supervised rewrite of Owen's essay this Thursday, November 12, after school, with its mark replacing the zero and nothing placed on his record. I still require a fixed date for the mark to be entered, not "well before December 1," and written confirmation of every term. I expect it in writing tonight.

Meredith Kalinowski

DEBRIEF
Where she ended: She reached her last position and agreed to a private supervised rewrite on Thursday, November 12 after school, with the mark replacing the zero and nothing on his record, all in writing tonight; she still wants a fixed date for the mark, and this is the fair outcome under procedure 4.4, reached with time to spare.
What moved her: You showed her the invented line from Act 3, Scene 2 with the play open to the page, because she could check it herself and it did not depend on anyone's say-so.
What cost ground: You opened with the detector score and called it conclusive, which let her dismiss your case as a machine's guess and made her cold from the start.
What she never said: In October she came downstairs at 1 AM and saw a ChatGPT window open on the family laptop, Owen closed it, and she never asked; your version history, with the document created late on October 28 and the big pastes minutes before midnight, came very close to that night, though it proves nothing about the essay itself and is why she pushed so hard.
Try next time: Start with your own admission about entering the zero early and go straight to the version history, so the detector score never becomes the first thing she gets to knock down.
